children.text: Summit Home Services was founded in 2009 by Mike Sullivan, a master plumber who spent 12 years working for large mechanical contractors before deciding Springfield homeowners deserved better -- honest pricing, same-day response, and technicians who explain what they're doing and why.
Our story

What started as Mike and a service van has grown into a team of 14 licensed technicians covering plumbing, HVAC, and electrical across Central Illinois. We've completed over 10,000 jobs and maintained a 4.9-star Google rating because we treat every home like our own.
How we work

Every call starts the same way: we listen, we show up on time, and we diagnose the problem before quoting a price. You'll never get a bill that's higher than the estimate. If we recommend a repair, we explain why it's needed and what happens if you wait. No pressure, no upselling, no games.
Built for Central Illinois

Illinois homes have unique challenges -- aging galvanized pipes in pre-war houses, furnaces that run hard through sub-zero winters, and AC systems that struggle through humid summers. Our techs are trained on the specific systems and conditions found in Central Illinois homes, from 1920s bungalows to new construction in Chatham.

data.title: 5 Signs Your Water Heater Needs Replacing
data.excerpt: Water heaters don't last forever. Here are five clear warning signs that yours is on its way out -- and what to do before it fails completely.

$media.alt: Water heater in a residential utility room

children.text: Your water heater works hard every day, heating 40-80 gallons of water for showers, dishes, and laundry. Most tank water heaters last 8-12 years, and tankless units can go 15-20. But when they start to fail, the signs are usually there if you know what to look for.
1. Your water heater is over 10 years old

Check the serial number on the manufacturer's label. Most brands encode the manufacture date in the first four digits. If your tank water heater is approaching 10 years, it's time to start planning for a replacement rather than waiting for it to fail -- usually at the worst possible moment.
2. Rusty or discolored water

If the hot water coming from your faucets has a rusty or brownish tint, the inside of your tank is corroding. Once the tank starts rusting from the inside, there's no repair -- it's only a matter of time before it develops a leak. Run three or four buckets of hot water. If the rust persists, it's the heater, not the pipes.
3. Rumbling or banging noises

Sediment builds up at the bottom of the tank over time, especially in areas with hard water. As the sediment layer thickens, the burner has to work harder to heat the water through it, causing rumbling and popping sounds. This wastes energy and accelerates wear on the tank.
4. Water pooling around the base

Any moisture or pooling around the base of your water heater is a red flag. Check the fittings and the temperature/pressure relief valve first -- those are fixable. But if the tank itself is leaking, replacement is the only option. Don't wait on this one.
5. Not enough hot water

If your showers are getting shorter because the hot water runs out faster than it used to, the heating elements or burner may be failing, or sediment buildup has reduced the tank's effective capacity. If your unit is also old, replacing it with a properly sized unit is usually the smarter investment.

If you're seeing any of these signs, give us a call. We'll inspect your current unit, explain your options -- tank vs. tankless, gas vs. electric -- and give you a straightforward quote. Same-day installation is available for most standard water heaters.

data.title: How to Prepare Your HVAC System for Summer
data.excerpt: A little spring maintenance goes a long way. Here's how to get your AC ready for the heat so it doesn't let you down in July.

$media.alt: Outdoor HVAC condenser unit next to a house

children.text: Central Illinois summers are no joke -- humidity, 90-degree days, and the occasional heat advisory mean your AC system needs to be in top shape before the season hits. Here's what you can do yourself and what's worth calling a pro for.
Change your filter

This is the single most important thing you can do. A clogged filter restricts airflow, makes your system work harder, drives up your electric bill, and can cause the evaporator coil to freeze. Change it every 1-3 months during cooling season.
Clear the area around your outdoor unit

Your condenser needs airflow to release heat. Clear any leaves, grass clippings, and debris from around the unit. Trim back plants and shrubs to maintain at least 2 feet of clearance on all sides. Gently hose off the condenser fins to remove built-up dirt.
Test your system before you need it

Turn on your AC on a mild spring day and let it run for 15-20 minutes. Check that cold air is coming from all vents, listen for unusual noises, and look for any water leaks around the indoor unit. Finding a problem now means you'll get it fixed on your schedule.
Schedule a professional tune-up

A professional maintenance visit covers things you can't easily do yourself: checking refrigerant levels, testing electrical connections, cleaning the evaporator coil, inspecting the blower motor, and verifying thermostat calibration. Annual maintenance extends the life of your system by 3-5 years on average. Our spring tune-up is $89 and takes about an hour.

data.title: When to Call a Plumber vs. DIY
data.excerpt: Some plumbing jobs are great DIY projects. Others will cost you more if you try them yourself. Here's how to know the difference.

$media.alt: Plumbing tools laid out on a work surface

children.text: YouTube has convinced a lot of homeowners that every plumbing job is a weekend project. Some are. But we also get a lot of calls that start with 'I tried to fix it myself and now it's worse.' Here's an honest breakdown of what's safe to tackle on your own and when it's smarter to call a professional.
Good DIY projects

Replacing a faucet or showerhead, unclogging a drain with a plunger or hand snake, replacing a toilet flapper or fill valve, installing a new toilet seat, replacing a washing machine hose, and fixing a running toilet. These jobs require basic tools and have low risk if something goes wrong.
Call a plumber

Anything involving the main sewer line, water heater installation or repair, gas line work (this requires a license by law), whole-house repiping, slab leaks, frozen pipe thawing (if not accessible), sump pump installation, and any job that requires a permit.
The gray area

Toilet replacement, garbage disposal installation, and under-sink plumbing modifications are in the middle. If you're comfortable with basic plumbing connections and have done similar work before, go for it. If it's your first time, consider having a plumber do it.

The best rule of thumb: if there's a shutoff valve between you and the problem, it's probably safe to try. If the only way to stop the water is to shut off the main, call a pro. And if you smell gas, leave the house and call your utility company immediately.

data.title: Springfield Victorian Whole-Home Repipe
data.summary: Complete replacement of galvanized steel pipes with PEX throughout a 2,400 sq ft 1920s Victorian, including 2 bathrooms, kitchen, and laundry -- all without damaging original plaster walls.

children.text: The Harrisons' 1920s Victorian had its original galvanized steel pipes, which were corroded, restricted, and causing low water pressure throughout the house. The challenge: repipe the entire home without damaging the original plaster walls and hardwood floors.
Scope

Full removal of galvanized supply lines and replacement with PEX tubing using a home-run manifold system. New shut-off valves at every fixture. Upgraded water main from 3/4-inch to 1-inch. Minimal wall openings patched and refinished to match existing plaster. Project completed in 4 days with water restored each evening.

data.title: Downtown Restaurant HVAC Replacement
data.summary: Replaced a failing 15-ton rooftop unit with two high-efficiency units and added a dedicated kitchen make-up air system -- completed during off-hours with zero lost business days.

$media.alt: Commercial building with rooftop HVAC units

children.text: Napoli's Italian Kitchen had been limping along with a 15-ton rooftop unit that was 22 years old and costing them over $800/month in repairs. The dining room was never the right temperature and the kitchen was unbearable in summer.
Result

We installed two 7.5-ton high-efficiency units with variable-speed compressors. Added a dedicated make-up air system for the kitchen hood. All work was done between 10 PM and 6 AM over two weeks. The restaurant's electric bill dropped 30% in the first full month.

data.title: Chatham Emergency Sewer Line Repair
data.summary: Emergency response to a complete sewer line collapse caused by tree root intrusion -- diagnosed with camera inspection and repaired with trenchless pipe bursting.

children.text: The Davis family called on a Saturday morning with sewage backing up into their basement. Our emergency crew arrived within an hour and ran a sewer camera to find the problem: a large oak tree's roots had collapsed a 15-foot section of the original clay sewer line.
Trenchless solution

We used pipe bursting -- a trenchless method that feeds a new HDPE pipe through the old one. We only needed two small access pits instead of a full trench. The new line is root-proof and carries a 50-year warranty. The job was completed in one day.
